title: Language translators, source code and object code

visuals.title: The journey of a C++ program: source to running

stages.name: Source code (program.cpp)
stages.detail: The C++ you type. Humans can read it, the CPU cannot run it.

stages.name: Preprocessor
stages.detail: Adds the #include files. The result is expanded code.

stages.name: Compiler
stages.detail: Translates the whole program and reports errors. Produces object code.

stages.name: Object code (program.obj / .o)
stages.detail: Machine code for your file only. It cannot run yet because library code (like cout) is missing.

stages.name: Linker
stages.detail: Joins your object code with library code, for example the code behind iostream.

stages.name: Executable (program.exe)
stages.detail: The final machine code that the CPU can run directly.

stages.name: Loader and run
stages.detail: The loader puts the program in RAM and the CPU executes it.

visuals.title: Match the translator or code type to its meaning

pairs.meaning: Translates the whole program at once and makes an .exe
Translates and runs one line at a time, no .exe
Converts assembly language into machine code
Compiler output that cannot run yet (.obj)

goal: After this you can explain why translators are needed. You can compare a compiler, an interpreter and an assembler. You can describe source, object and machine code, and tell syntax, runtime and logical errors apart.
warmup: Imagine you only speak Urdu and you must give directions to a driver who only understands Chinese. You need a translator. A computer's CPU understands only machine language (0s and 1s). Your C++ is written for humans. So we need a translator program in between.
definition: A language translator is a program that converts code written in one language into machine language. There are three kinds. A compiler translates a whole high-level program at once and creates an executable file. An interpreter translates and runs the program one line at a time. An assembler converts assembly language into machine code. Source code is the program you write (.cpp). Object code is the compiler's machine-code output for your file only (.obj or .o). Machine code or the executable is the final code after linking (.exe) that the CPU can run.
howItWorks: C++ is a compiled language. The path has five steps. First, program.cpp (the source code) goes to the preprocessor, which adds the #include files. Second, the compiler translates it into object code (program.obj). Third, the linker joins the object code with library code (for example, the code behind cout) to make program.exe. Fourth, the loader places the program in RAM. Fifth, the CPU runs it. The compiler reports all syntax errors after it reads the whole program. An interpreter (Python, JavaScript) stops at the first error. It creates no .exe, and it translates again every time, so it is usually slower. There are three kinds of error. A syntax error breaks a language rule and is caught at compile time. A runtime error happens while the program runs (for example, dividing by zero). A logical error lets the program run but gives a wrong answer.

worked.problem: A logical error. This program is meant to find the average of 10 and 20 (it should print 15). It compiles and runs, but what does it print? Why is it wrong?

sample.title: A logical error

explanation.text: The bug is here. Division happens before addition, so this is a + (b / 2) = 10 + 10 = 20, not 15. The compiler cannot see this mistake because the line is valid C++.
The wrong value is printed. Only testing reveals a logical error.

steps.note: b / 2 = 10 happens first, then 10 + 10 = 20. The expected 15 is not produced.
The program ends without any error message.

worked.problem: Debugging question: the program above has a logical error. Write the corrected program that reads two marks and prints their average correctly. (Test with 10 and 20: the answer must be 15.)

sample.title: Corrected average

explanation.text: Read the two marks: 10 into a and 20 into b.
Brackets make the addition happen first: (10 + 20) = 30. Dividing by 2.0 (a decimal) keeps any decimal part, so 30 / 2.0 = 15.

variations.when: Translates the whole program at once, reports all errors, makes an .exe (C, C++)
Translates and runs line by line, stops at the first error, no .exe (Python, JavaScript)
Converts assembly language to machine code
A language rule is broken; found at compile time
Found while the program runs; it may crash
Program runs but gives a wrong answer

mistakes.error: expected ';' before 'return' (a syntax error, found by the compiler)
Compiles without error, but the program crashes when run (a runtime error). The exact crash message depends on the system.
No message at all. It compiles and runs but prints a wrong answer (a logical error).
'x' was not declared in this scope

examTips: Compiler = whole program at once, creates an executable, reports all errors. Interpreter = line by line, no executable, stops at the first error. Assembler = assembly to machine code.
Source code (.cpp) is human-readable. Object code (.obj) is the compiler's output and cannot run alone. The executable (.exe) is machine code after linking.
Learn the journey: .cpp, preprocessor, compiler, .obj, linker, .exe, loader, execution.
Syntax error = at compile time. Runtime error = while running (for example dividing by zero). Logical error = wrong answer, no crash. Give one example of each.
Compiled programs run faster because they are already translated. Interpreters translate every time.
romanSummary: CPU sirf machine language samajhta hai, is liye translator chahiye.
Compiler poora program ek saath translate karke .exe banata hai (C++). Interpreter ek ek line chalata hai (Python). Assembler assembly ko machine code banata hai.
Source code (.cpp) hum likhte hain, compiler usay object code (.obj) banata hai, linker library ke saath jor kar .exe banata hai.
Errors 3 qisam ke hain: syntax (compile pe), runtime (chalte waqt crash), logical (galat answer).

practice.prompt: Which translator converts the whole program at once?
practice.explanation: A compiler translates the entire program and creates an executable.

practice.prompt: Fill in the blank: the file you write in C++ is called ______ code.
practice.explanation: Source code is the human-readable program written by the programmer.

practice.prompt: Which file can the CPU run directly?
practice.hint: It is the final result of linking.
practice.explanation: The executable (.exe) holds the final machine code.

options: Joins object code with library code
practice.answer: Joins object code with library code
practice.hint: It makes the object code complete.
practice.explanation: The linker adds library code (like the code behind cout) to your object code to make the executable.

practice.hint: endl moves to a new line after B.
practice.explanation: A and B are printed on the same line because the first cout has no endl. Then endl starts a new line, and C is printed on the second line.
A missing semicolon breaks a language rule, so it is a syntax error found during compilation.

practice.prompt: Write one-line examples of a syntax error, a runtime error and a logical error in C++.
practice.answer:
Syntax error: cout << "Hi"   (missing ;)
Runtime error: int c = a / 0;   (division by zero while running)
Logical error: avg = a + b / 2;   (wrong answer, should be (a + b) / 2)
practice.hint: Think: compile time, run time, wrong answer.
practice.explanation: Each error kind appears at a different time: syntax at compile time, runtime while running, logical in the answer.

practice.prompt: Which statement about an interpreter is true?
options: It stops at the first error and creates no .exe
It is faster than a compiler at running
practice.answer: It stops at the first error and creates no .exe
practice.explanation: An interpreter translates and executes one line at a time, so it stops at the first error.
